questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: 3.5 (Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis), 1.5 (Growth and evolution), 1.4 (Stakeholders)
questions.subtopic: 3.5 / 1.5 / 1.4 Ratio analysis applied to a growth decision
questions.challenge_mechanism: The ratio analysis looks uniformly healthy, so the student has to notice that the question is not whether the business is strong but which growth model converts that strength into return without consuming the balance sheet that produced it.

stimulus.title: Maren & Daughters
stimulus.body: Maren & Daughters is a family-owned chain of twelve bakery cafés in a medium-sized European city. It is owned entirely by the founder's three children, who work in the business and take all major decisions between them. The chain has grown steadily by opening one new café roughly every eighteen months, each funded from retained profit and a bank loan. The bank has now indicated that it will not lend further without additional security. Two of the three owners want to grow by franchising; the third wants to continue opening company-owned cafés and is prepared to bring in an outside investor. Extracts from the most recent accounts are given below, together with the projections prepared by each camp.

table.caption: Extracts from the most recent accounts and the two projections
rows: net profit after interest and tax
franchise option: 40 outlets, upfront fee each
company-owned option: 8 new cafés, capital cost each
company-owned option: annual operating profit each

questions.question: Using the case study and the figures provided, answer all three parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the recent financial performance and position of Maren & Daughters using ratio analysis. Your analysis must include calculations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Maren & Daughters should expand by franchising or by opening company-owned cafés, using the projections in the case study.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss the likely impact of the expansion on two different stakeholder groups, and explain why their interests may conflict.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Gross profit is $8.40-3.78=\unicode{8364}4.62$ m, so the gross margin is $\dfrac{4.62}{8.40}=55.0\%$. **(M1)(A1)** Operating profit is $4.62-3.36=\unicode{8364}1.26$ m, an operating margin of $15.0\%$, and the net margin is $\dfrac{0.756}{8.40}=9.0\%$. **(A1)** Return on capital employed is $\dfrac{1.26}{6.30}=20.0\%$, which is strong for a retail food business and suggests the existing estate is being used well. **(A1)** Liquidity looks comfortable: the current ratio is $\dfrac{1.68}{0.84}=2.0$, well above the usual benchmark of $1.5$. **(A1)** Gearing is $\dfrac{2.52}{6.30}=40\%$, which is not alarming in itself but matters here because the bank has already refused further lending without security. **(A1)** The overall picture is a profitable, liquid business whose constraint is access to capital rather than the quality of its trading. **(R1)**

**(b)** Franchising generates $\unicode{8364}1.0$ m in upfront fees $(40\times\unicode{8364}25\,000)$ and $\unicode{8364}1.44$ m a year in royalties $(40\times6\%\times\unicode{8364}600\,000)$. **(M1)(A1)** It requires almost no capital, it sidesteps the bank's refusal entirely, and it transfers most of the operating risk to the franchisees. **(A1)** Against that, the royalty stream is only as good as the franchisees: sixty per cent of the chain's future profit would depend on people the family does not employ and cannot directly manage, and one café cutting corners on hygiene would damage a brand built over twenty years. The $\unicode{8364}1.0$ m of fees is also one-off, so the recurring benefit is the $\unicode{8364}1.44$ m royalty, not the headline $\unicode{8364}2.44$ m. **(A1)**

The company-owned option costs $8\times\unicode{8364}450\,000=\unicode{8364}3.6$ m and adds $8\times\unicode{8364}90\,000=\unicode{8364}0.72$ m a year before depreciation, or about $\unicode{8364}0.36$ m after charging depreciation over ten years. **(M1)(A1)** Payback is $\dfrac{3.6}{0.72}=5$ years, and the return on the new capital is roughly $10\%$, which is half the $20\%$ the business currently earns. **(A1)**

On the figures, franchising dominates: it produces more annual income, needs a fraction of the capital, and avoids diluting ownership. **(R1)** The qualification is that the comparison is not purely financial. Franchising converts a business the family controls into one it licenses, and the loss of control over standards is the genuine cost, not the lost margin. A balanced evaluation therefore recommends franchising but with a contractual and operational framework — approved suppliers, inspection rights, a training requirement — that protects the brand, and possibly a small number of company-owned cafés retained as a benchmark and a training base. **(R1)**

**(c)** *The three owner-directors.* Under franchising they keep full ownership and receive fees and royalties without new borrowing, so income rises and personal financial risk falls. **(M1)(A1)** However, the third sibling's objection is not about money but about control, and two of them will get their way over the third, which risks a family relationship as well as a business one. **(A1)**

*Employees.* Under franchising the existing staff keep their jobs but the new outlets' staff are employed by franchisees, probably on different terms and without the informal culture of a family firm; there is also no longer a clear promotion ladder into new cafés. Under the company-owned route about eighty new jobs are created inside the business with the same terms and progression. **(M1)(A1)**

The interests conflict because owners benefit from franchising's lower risk and faster income while employees benefit from the company-owned route's job creation and internal promotion. **(A1)** A candidate might also note that customers gain from faster expansion under either option but lose if franchise standards slip, which links the stakeholder analysis back to the brand risk identified in (b). **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) award one mark per correctly calculated and interpreted ratio, up to a maximum of four; candidates must calculate rather than describe. Accept other valid ratios such as the acid test or the gearing ratio expressed against equity, provided they are computed from the figures given. The ROCE figure is the one that matters most, because the whole question turns on whether new capital earns the 20% the business currently earns. In (b) the evaluation mark requires a supported judgement; a balanced list of advantages with no conclusion is capped at four. Candidates who prefer the company-owned route should not be penalised provided they engage with the 10% versus 20% return and the capital constraint imposed by the bank, since the bank's refusal is what makes the option difficult rather than impossible. In (c) any two stakeholder groups are acceptable, but the conflict must be identified explicitly rather than left implicit in two separate descriptions.  Candidates who argue for a mixed strategy — a small core of company-owned cafés retained for training and benchmarking alongside a franchised estate — should be credited, and arguably deserve credit above a pure recommendation, because it addresses the control objection without abandoning the capital advantage. Where a candidate raises the outside investor as a third option, allow it on its merits; the case study does not quantify it, which is a legitimate point to make rather than an omission to be penalised.
questions.explanation: The case study is constructed so that the financial analysis and the strategic conclusion pull in different directions, which is what makes it worth fifteen marks. Every ratio a candidate computes in (a) is healthy — 55% gross margin, 20% ROCE, a current ratio of 2.0 — and the tempting conclusion is that the business is doing well and should carry on as it is. The bank's refusal to lend is the one fact that breaks that reading, and it is buried in the stimulus rather than highlighted, so candidates have to notice it for themselves. Once noticed, it reframes the whole question: the constraint is capital, not capability, and that is precisely the situation in which franchising beats organic growth. Part (b) then adds a second wrinkle, because the recurring royalty of €1.44m is genuinely attractive while the €1.0m of upfront fees is not recurring at all, and a candidate who treats €2.44m as an annual figure has misread the model. The evaluation is not simply 'franchising wins': the real cost is loss of control over brand standards, which no ratio captures, and the strongest answers say so and propose a safeguard.  A second teaching point is worth drawing out of (b) if there is time afterwards. The €1.0m of franchise fees is a one-off receipt while the €1.44m royalty recurs, and the difference between the two is exactly the difference between selling an asset and building an income stream. Candidates routinely add them together, and the habit of asking whether a figure recurs is one that transfers directly to cash-flow forecasting and to investment appraisal, where a terminal receipt and an annual saving must never be summed.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. Figures chosen so that every headline ratio is comfortable while the bank's lending refusal creates the actual constraint, and so that the company-owned option returns exactly half the current ROCE.

verification.method: All ratios and projections recomputed in Python; the royalty stream, the capital cost, the payback period and the return on new capital checked independently.
solution_skeleton: compute margin, return and liquidity ratios from the extracts
identify the binding constraint from the narrative rather than the ratios
compare the two growth models on recurring income and capital required
weigh the unquantified cost of losing operational control
trace the consequences for two stakeholder groups and surface the conflict

questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.subtopic: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
questions.challenge_mechanism: The headline unit-cost comparison says reshoring is a mistake, and the student has to find the two effects that are not in the unit cost — the working capital released by a shorter lead time and the markdowns avoided — before the decision can be judged.

stimulus.title: Vantar
stimulus.body: Vantar makes technical outdoor clothing. It currently manufactures 180 000 units a year in a low-wage economy and sells them online and through a small number of independent retailers at a retail price of €59. The lead time from placing an order to having stock available is 62 days, which forces Vantar to commit to its whole season's production before it knows what will sell. The operations director has costed a move to a domestic factory: the unit production cost would be higher, but the lead time would fall to 9 days, which would allow the company to make small reorders during the season. The finance director has calculated that the average value of finished-goods stock would fall from €2.10m to €0.72m, and the company's annual cost of holding stock is 18% of its value. Vantar's marketing manager estimates that 4% of units are currently sold at an average markdown of 35% because the wrong sizes were committed to. The cost data are given below.

questions.question: Using the case study and the cost data, answer all three parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total landed cost per unit for the offshore option and for the domestic option, and calculate the increase in annual production cost if Vantar reshores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether Vantar should move production to the domestic factory, taking into account the effect on stockholding and the markdowns described in the case study.

parts.label: c
parts.text: To what extent do factors other than cost determine the right decision for Vantar? Refer to at least two external factors in your answer.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Offshore: $\text{CIF}=14.00+1.20=\unicode{8364}15.20$; the tariff is $12\%$ of $\unicode{8364}15.20=\unicode{8364}1.82$; adding $\unicode{8364}0.30$ handling gives a landed cost of $\unicode{8364}17.32$ per unit. **(M1)(A1)** Domestic: $21.50+0.25=\unicode{8364}21.75$ per unit. **(A1)** The increase is $\unicode{8364}4.43$ per unit, so across $180\,000$ units the annual production cost rises by $4.426\times180\,000=\unicode{8364}796\,680$, about $\unicode{8364}797\,000$. **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** On unit cost alone the move looks wrong: $\unicode{8364}4.43$ is a $25.5\%$ increase in the cost of every item. **(A1)** Two effects work against that conclusion. First, average stock falls from $\unicode{8364}2.10$ m to $\unicode{8364}0.72$ m, a release of $\unicode{8364}1.38$ m, and at an annual holding cost of $18\%$ that saves $1.38\times0.18=\unicode{8364}248\,400$ a year. **(M1)(A1)** Second, a nine-day lead time allows reorders during the season rather than a single pre-commitment, so the markdown problem largely disappears: $4\%$ of $180\,000$ units is $7\,200$ units, currently discounted by $35\%$ of $\unicode{8364}59$, which is about $\unicode{8364}148\,700$ of lost margin a year. **(M1)(A1)** Together these recover about $\unicode{8364}397\,000$, so the net additional cost is roughly $\unicode{8364}797\,000-\unicode{8364}397\,000=\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year, or $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit — about $3.8\%$ of the $\unicode{8364}59$ retail price, not the $25\%$ headline figure. **(A1)**

Against that residual cost must be set a shorter cash cycle, far less risk of being left with a season's worth of unwanted stock, and the marketing value of being able to promote a domestic supply chain. **(A1)** A balanced evaluation is that the move is financially defensible if Vantar can recover $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit through a modest price rise or through the higher full-price sell-through that reordering makes possible, and it is not defensible if the market will not bear any increase at all. The decisive question is therefore not cost but price elasticity, which the data do not give. **(R1)**

**(c)** To a considerable extent, because the cost gap after the stock and markdown effects is small enough that external factors can easily dominate it. **(A1)** *Political:* the offshore option depends on a $12\%$ tariff that a trade dispute could raise overnight; a five-point increase would add about $\unicode{8364}0.76$ to every unit and close a third of the remaining gap by itself, and this risk is entirely outside Vantar's control. **(M1)(A1)** *Environmental and ethical:* the company sells technical outdoor clothing to customers who are unusually attentive to provenance, and a domestic supply chain with a much shorter transport leg is a marketing asset that does not appear in the cost comparison at all; conversely, moving production offshore to a jurisdiction with weaker labour protections would carry reputational risk that could cost more than $\unicode{8364}400\,000$. **(M1)(A1)** *Economic:* a domestic factory removes exposure to freight-cost volatility and to currency movement on a $\unicode{8364}2.52$ m annual import bill. **(A1)** The counter-argument is that $\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year is real money and that none of these factors is certain, so the decision remains finely balanced; but where the quantified gap is under four per cent of retail price, factors that cannot be quantified will usually decide it. **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) allow €17.30 to €17.35 and €21.70 to €21.80, and credit the tariff calculation shown even if the final addition is wrong. The annual increase should be about €797,000; allow €795,000 to €800,000. In (b) the evaluation mark requires the candidate to bring in both the stockholding saving and the markdown saving; an evaluation based on unit cost alone is capped at three, and one based on unit cost plus stockholding but not markdowns is capped at four. Allow a range of about €390,000 to €410,000 for the net cost, since candidates may treat the markdown recovery differently. In (c) any two of the STEEPLE factors are acceptable provided each is applied to Vantar specifically rather than described in the abstract; a generic list of external factors with no application earns at most two marks.  In (b) a candidate may reasonably question the 18% holding cost or the assumption that the whole stock reduction is achieved in the first year; both are fair challenges and should be credited where they are explained, since the case study presents them as estimates rather than facts. Do not, however, credit a rejection of the markdown saving on the grounds that it is uncertain: it is quantified in the stimulus and is the whole reason the lead-time reduction has value.
questions.explanation: The item is built around a gap between the number a student computes first and the number that matters. The unit-cost comparison — €17.32 against €21.75 — is unambiguous and points one way, and a candidate who stops there concludes that reshoring is obviously wrong. The two effects that reverse the picture are both in the stimulus rather than in the cost table: €1.38m of stock is released, worth €248,400 a year at an 18% holding cost, and 53 days of lead time are removed, which is what allows the markdown problem to be solved at all. Neither appears in a unit cost, and that is the point — a landed-cost calculation systematically excludes working capital and obsolescence, both of which can exceed the cost difference it is being used to measure. Part (c) then asks the candidate to weigh factors that cannot be quantified against a residual gap of about €2.22 per unit, and the honest answer is that a gap of under four per cent of retail price is small enough that a tariff change or a reputational effect could overturn it. That is a genuinely transferable conclusion about offshoring decisions and is why the figures were calibrated to produce it.  The item also rewards candidates who notice what the data do not contain. Nothing in the case study says how price-sensitive Vantar's customers are, and the entire recommendation rests on it: if the market will absorb €2.22 then the move is straightforward, and if it will not then the move destroys value. Naming the missing variable, and saying what it would take to find it out, is a stronger answer than any amount of further arithmetic on the figures already given.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. Costs chosen so the landed-cost gap is 25.5% while the stock and markdown effects recover half of it, leaving a residual of about 4% of retail price that external factors could plausibly overturn.

verification.method: Landed costs, annual cost increase, stockholding saving, markdown recovery and net residual all recomputed in Python.
solution_skeleton: build the landed cost from production, freight, tariff and handling elements
scale the unit difference to an annual figure
value the working-capital release at the stated holding cost
value the markdown reduction enabled by the shorter lead time
compare the residual gap with external factors that cannot be quantified
